subChunks.title: useMemo and useCallback — Memoisation Explained
subChunks.hookHtml: useMemo and useCallback are optimisation hooks. Used incorrectly, they add complexity without benefit. Used correctly, they prevent expensive recalculations and unnecessary child re-renders. The key insight: both are about referential stability, and you almost never need them until you have measured a real performance problem — but you need to understand them to reason about React's render behaviour.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
useMemo — cache an expensive computation

useMemo runs a function and caches its result. It only re-runs when the specified dependencies change:

import { useMemo } from 'react';

function FilteredList({ items, filterText }) {
  // Without useMemo: filter runs on EVERY render (including unrelated state changes)
  // With useMemo: filter only runs when items or filterText changes
  const filtered = useMemo(
    () => items.filter(item => item.name.toLowerCase().includes(filterText.toLowerCase())),
    [items, filterText]
  );

  return <ul>{filtered.map(i => <li key={i.id}>{i.name}</li>)}</ul>;
}

For a list of 10 items, this is overkill — the computation is instant. For 10,000 items with a complex predicate, it matters.

useMemo — stabilising object references

Even with small data, useMemo is useful when the result is passed as a prop to a memoised child or as a dependency to another hook:

// ❌ Without useMemo: options is a new object every render
// even if a and b haven't changed:
const options = { a: propA, b: propB };

// ✅ With useMemo: options is the same reference when propA and propB are unchanged:
const options = useMemo(() => ({ a: propA, b: propB }), [propA, propB]);

useCallback — stable function references

useCallback caches a function, returning the same function reference between renders unless its dependencies change:

import { useCallback } from 'react';

function Parent({ itemId }) {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

  // ❌ Without useCallback: new function reference every render:
  const handleDelete = () => deleteItem(itemId);

  // ✅ With useCallback: same reference when itemId hasn't changed:
  const handleDelete = useCallback(() => {
    deleteItem(itemId);
  }, [itemId]);

  return <ChildButton onClick={handleDelete} count={count} />;
}

When these hooks matter

useMemo and useCallback are only worthwhile when:

  1. The computation is genuinely expensive (sorting/filtering thousands of items)
  2. The value/function is passed to a React.memo-wrapped child — otherwise the child re-renders regardless
  3. The value is a dependency of another hook (useEffect, useMemo) and you want to prevent infinite loops

They are not a general cure for slow components. Profile first (React DevTools Profiler), then optimise.

Vex: "Every useMemo and useCallback adds overhead: memory for the cached value, time to compare dependencies, cognitive overhead to understand why it's there. Add them only when you have measured a problem. Premature memoisation is as harmful as premature optimisation."

The mental model

// useMemo: "give me the same value unless these things change"
const result = useMemo(() => expensive(a, b), [a, b]);

// useCallback: "give me the same function unless these things change"
const fn = useCallback(() => doSomething(x), [x]);

// useCallback is useMemo for functions:
// useCallback(fn, deps) === useMemo(() => fn, deps)

storyBeats.text: Vex points to a cauldron that re-brews the same potion every second — even when the ingredients haven't changed. 'Wasteful,' she says. 'The magic should remember the last brew and only work again when something actually changed.'

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: Both hooks are about referential stability. useMemo remembers a value. useCallback remembers a function. The dependency array tells React when the memory is stale. Neither is free — add them only when you've measured a real problem.

storyBeats.speaker: useMemo vs no memo

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Build a <SortableList items /> component:

  • State: sortOrder ('asc' or 'desc') and an unrelated count
  • Use useMemo to sort items by name — sorted list only recomputes when items or sortOrder changes
  • Render the sorted items in a <ul data-testid="list">
  • A toggle button switches between asc/desc
  • A separate 'Ping' button increments count — verify (via a log) that sorting doesn't re-run on count change

guidedPracticeTests.label: First item is Aria in asc order

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Build a <ProductSearch products /> component from scratch. State: searchText and an unrelated theme toggle. Use useMemo for filtering products by name. Use useCallback for the search input handler. Toggling the theme should not re-run the filter (verify via console.log inside useMemo). Show the filtered count.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain useMemo and useCallback to a developer who has never seen them. What problem do they solve? What's the difference between them? Give an example of when NOT to use them — and what the actual cost of overusing them is.

questions.prompt: What does `useMemo(() => expensiveCalc(a, b), [a, b])` do?
options: Caches the result of expensiveCalc — only re-runs when a or b changes
Runs expensiveCalc before every render and caches the result
Runs expensiveCalc asynchronously and updates state when done
Prevents the component from re-rendering when a or b changes
questions.answer: Caches the result of expensiveCalc — only re-runs when a or b changes
questions.explanation: useMemo computes the value on first render, then returns the cached value on subsequent renders unless a or b has changed. It does not prevent re-renders — the component still re-renders; it just skips the expensive computation if the inputs are unchanged.

questions.prompt: What is the relationship between useCallback and useMemo?
options: useCallback(fn, deps) is equivalent to useMemo(() => fn, deps) — they both cache a value, but useCallback specialises in functions
useCallback is faster than useMemo because it skips the closure creation step
useMemo is for synchronous values; useCallback is for asynchronous functions
They are unrelated — useCallback manages side effects, useMemo manages state
questions.answer: useCallback(fn, deps) is equivalent to useMemo(() => fn, deps) — they both cache a value, but useCallback specialises in functions
questions.explanation: useCallback is syntactic sugar over useMemo specifically for function values. Both cache their return value and only recompute when dependencies change. useCallback(fn, deps) === useMemo(() => fn, deps).

questions.prompt: When should you add useMemo to a component?
options: When you have measured via the Profiler that a specific computation is causing performance problems in a real use case
For any computation that runs during render — as a precaution
Whenever a variable is used as a prop to avoid child re-renders
Any time the component re-renders more than once per second
questions.answer: When you have measured via the Profiler that a specific computation is causing performance problems in a real use case
questions.explanation: useMemo adds memory, dependency comparison overhead, and cognitive complexity. For most computations (even sorting small arrays), it costs more than it saves. Profile first with React DevTools Profiler. Then add useMemo only where measurement shows a specific computation is the bottleneck.
